title: How beer is made
lead: Four ingredients and one long day of brewing, then weeks of waiting.

sections.name: Four ingredients
know: Malt: sugar, color and most of the flavor.
Yeast turns sugar into alcohol and bubbles.
sections.source: Cicerone, US Certified Beer Server Syllabus v6.0, 2024 (cicerone.org)

sections.name: Malt

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Grain that’s sprouted, then dried in a kiln.

know: The longer and hotter the kiln, the darker the malt.
Pale tastes like bread; dark like coffee.

sections.name: Brew day
know: The mash turns starch into sugar.
Early hops add bitterness; late hops add aroma.
Dry hopping adds aroma without bitterness.
sections.source: Cicerone, US Certified Beer Server Syllabus v6.0, 2024 (cicerone.org); CraftBeer.com (Brewers Association), Beer Glossary

sections.name: Ale or lager
know: Ale yeast works warmer and makes fruity flavors.
Lager yeast works cooler and tastes clean.
sections.source: Cicerone, US Certified Beer Server Syllabus v6.0, 2024 (cicerone.org); American Homebrewers Association, “Ale vs. Lager: What’s the Difference?” (homebrewersassociation.org)

sections.name: Corn, rice, gluten-free and NA

lines.label: In short
lines.text: What’s on some labels, and what it means.

know: American lagers can use corn or rice to keep them light.
Gluten-free uses no barley or wheat; gluten-reduced does.
sections.source: BJCP 2021 Style Guidelines, 1A and 1B (bjcp.org); Cicerone, US Certified Beer Server Syllabus v6.0, 2024 (cicerone.org)

keyPoints.line: sugar, color, most of the flavor.

read.bigIdea: Almost every beer is four things.
read.where: **Malted grain** gives the sugar, the color and most of the flavor. **Hops** give bitterness, flavor and aroma. **Yeast** turns the sugar into **alcohol**, **CO2** and flavor. **Water** is more than **90%** of the beer, and its minerals shape the taste.
read.mixup: Hops aren’t a grain. They’re the flowers of a climbing plant.

read.bigIdea: The malt’s color is the beer’s flavor.
read.where: **Malt** is grain, usually **barley**, that’s soaked, allowed to **sprout**, then **dried in a kiln**. The hotter and longer it’s kilned or roasted, the **darker** it gets. Cicerone ties color to flavor: **pale** beers taste like bread dough or crackers, **amber** like toast or caramel, **brown** like nuts or chocolate, **black** like roast or coffee.
read.mixup: Dark doesn’t mean strong. A dry Irish stout is lighter in alcohol than most IPAs.
read.sayIt: It’s a dark beer, but it drinks light: coffee and chocolate, not heavy.

keyPoints.line: hot water turns starch into sugar.
early hops bitter, late hops aroma.

read.bigIdea: Sugar first, then hops, then yeast.
read.where: The malt is milled and **mashed** in hot water so its enzymes turn **starch into sugar**. The sweet liquid (**wort**) is drained off and **boiled with hops**. Hops added **early** give **bitterness**; hops added **late** give **flavor and aroma**. After chilling, the yeast goes in to **ferment**. **Dry hopping** adds hops after the boil, in the tank, for aroma without more bitterness (DDH on a label = double dry hopped).
read.mixup: A very hoppy-smelling beer isn’t always very bitter. Hazy IPAs are dry-hopped heavily but often less bitter.

read.bigIdea: Ale and lager are two families of yeast.
read.where: **Ale** yeast ferments **warmer** (roughly 60–70°F, some sources say up to 78°F) and makes **fruity** flavors, sometimes spicy ones. **Lager** yeast ferments **cooler** (roughly 45–58°F) and makes very little of either, so lagers taste of **malt and hops**: clean and crisp. Lagers are then **cold-aged** (“lagered”) for weeks.
read.mixup: Lager isn’t a color. There are pale lagers and black lagers; it’s the yeast that makes it a lager.
read.sayIt: It’s a lager, so it’s clean and crisp.

keyPoints.line: corn or rice keep American lager light.
no barley or wheat at all.

read.where: American lager and light lager can use **corn or rice** (up to about 40%) with barley malt, which keeps the body **light**. **Gluten-free** beer uses only gluten-free grains like sorghum or rice. **Gluten-reduced** beer is made from barley or wheat and treated: it isn’t gluten-free. **Non-alcoholic** means under **0.5% ABV**; **alcohol-free** means **0.0**.
read.mixup: “Gluten-reduced” isn’t safe for a guest with celiac. Only gluten-free is. When unsure, tell the guest and offer something else.
read.sayIt: That one is gluten-reduced, not gluten-free. For a gluten allergy I’d steer you to a cider or wine.

sources: Cicerone, US Certified Beer Server Syllabus v6.0, 2024 (cicerone.org); CraftBeer.com (Brewers Association), Beer Glossary; American Homebrewers Association, “Ale vs. Lager: What’s the Difference?” (homebrewersassociation.org); BJCP 2021 Style Guidelines, 1A American Light Lager, 1B American Lager (bjcp.org). Checked Nov 8, 2026.
